name: Notes and knowledge base
summary: Writing a thought down fast, finding what you need in an old archive and carrying on with the material — from lecture notes to a manuscript or the outcome of a meeting.
lead:
A new notepad is easy to keep in order: a handful of entries are visible all at once. A year later it holds work conversations, photos of a whiteboard, other people’s links and thoughts whose titles are hard to recall. From that point on, the value of a notes app depends on whether you can get back to your own material.

The reviews show two speeds: starting to write, and finding what was written. Between them lies the product’s main work — to save the entry, give it a place that makes sense and not lock it inside the app. For studying, for meetings and for long-form writing this shared path ends differently; specializing makes sense exactly where the material is needed again.

audiencesArt.alt: Different jobs in the “Notes and knowledge base” category.

audiences.title: Writing on the move
audiences.body: The thought arrives between other things. It has to be saved before any folder or title is chosen, and a short reminder can be left on the home screen if you want one.

audiences.title: Finding it in the pile
audiences.body: The person remembers a phrase, the other person in the conversation or a drawing on the page, but not the title. What they need is a path to the right place and the ability to take the archive with them when they change tools.

audiences.title: Using the material further on
audiences.body: After a meeting you need an outcome, after a lecture a review session, out of sketches a manuscript. The form the entry takes should help with that next action.

sections.title: Saving the thought before it disappears
sections.intro: People reach for a notes app in all sorts of circumstances: a short thought on the move, a lecture with a tablet, a long text in the evening. A shared blank page does not mean a shared scenario. The form of entry is worth choosing by what is going on around the note.

observations.title: Write first, pick the folder afterwards
passages: A quick note is needed at the moment when the thought has not taken shape yet. Choosing a folder, a template and a category forces you to organize something that isn’t there yet. Better to let people write first and offer to move or name it afterwards. This is most noticeable in the short turns to the phone between other things.

If a quick notepad requires a long walk through navigation, it has to be opened before the thought is even written down. Notes disappearing without any action you can point to undermines the very habit of trusting it with short entries. Save first, sort later is a more definite job than offering one more set of stickers.

The widget has a different role: to remind you without opening the editor. Someone may want to see only one phrase out of a long note, so the fragment on display has to be chosen separately. Fast capture and display on the home screen can sit side by side, but they don’t replace each other. Next we look at one more way out — passing what was written into the working tool you already use.

quotes.text: Alright, I've been trying different Note apps and for sure I have to say this is the best one I've used. It's simple to use and very quick to access and all.

After spending several hours test driving various sticky note apps, I frankly gave up the notion of ever finding one to my liking. The ones I tried were too time consuming in respect to navigation, they would delete notes on their own, they were not very well laid out

I love this app. I post positive quotes and Bible verses on my phone and can see them as soon as I unlock my screen. I do have two requests. 1. You can select a portion of your note to become the widget.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Write first, pick the folder afterwards”.

observations.title: Adding order once it is needed
passages: A simple notepad gets cramped once the topics in it are already hard to tell apart. But moving to tags, links and markup means learning a new system exactly when you want to just keep writing. Good organization helps answer a specific question; it doesn’t start with studying everything the editor can do.

Tags make more sense once someone is already trying to gather several entries on one topic. At that point an “add to project” action explains the structure better than an empty system of rules. New ways of organizing have to leave the old fast entry available, otherwise order is bought at the price of the basic habit of writing.

Markdown markup does not suit everyone. Someone who cares more about the content needs an ordinary editor and links between notes that make sense. Links are worth introducing at the moment the person is looking for neighboring material; a large graph on its own does not explain what to write down or how to come back to it.

quotes.text: I've been looking for a notes app for a long time that scratches the itch I have to keep things synced and organized. I moved from Google Keep which was OK but was missing some serious organization and power.

The first time I tried this app I got overwhelmed, it felt like the tags were fussy and I wasn't sure how to organize stuff. This was when I first got apple products and was seeking a notes app. Then I slowly worked my way through all the features.

Maybe it's just the way our brains age, but I'm a 40yo well-educated professional in technology and education and this app is incredibly intimidating. If you don't already work in markdown this may not be the best place to start.

placements.title: Adding order once it is needed

observations.title: Finding a page written by hand
passages: A free page lets you write, draw and place thoughts side by side straight away. Decoration can be part of the content of a personal entry too: color and visual detail help give a page a character of its own. What matters at the start is short preparation and comfortable pen movement, with no need to assemble a layout first.

Once the pages pile up, another job appears — an overview. A beautiful canvas is not enough if an earlier entry has to be found by long scrolling. Show convenient thumbnails and ways of moving between pages. Test not only the first note but also the return to the right place in a large handwritten notebook.

Visual details can help people recognize their pages and settle into them. But a review about fonts and colors is not yet confirmation that searching handwriting is convenient. A notebook needs both levels: pleasant writing and a way back to a specific place. Thumbnails, bookmarks and search across recognized words can be combined while the original placement of the marks is kept.

quotes.text: There are a few good apps that are devoted exclusively to handwriting -- that is, they do not also include a capability for typing. Because their use requires a minimum of set-up activity, these are the apps that you grab when you need to just get something down.

Beautiful app. Writes beautifully as well. But practically speaking, I could not use this for serious note taking. I take pages and pages of notes on a regular basis. That means I need a way to scroll through past notes efficiently.

I love this note app so much, I use it as my main notes app. The customization is amazing, and it’s very cute. So many fonts, backgrounds, font sizes, bold, underline, colors etc. It’s really useful and visually pleasing too. I hope the dev

sections.title: Coming back to what has already been written
sections.intro: After the first few dozen entries the way back becomes important. The person remembers the gist, but may forget the folder, the date and the exact wording. And if the entry can’t be found, they still have to work out whether the text is lost or only the path to it.

observations.title: Searching by memory, not by file name
passages: A single place for entries removes the first question: where to put a thought when its later fate is still unclear. That habit saves you from choosing an app every time. But the promise of “write it down and forget it” only works when there is a way back — the person has to find the material when it is needed.

A long-form writer needs a library where they can return both to an old sketch and to the current chapter. A search result should open the fragment in question and keep its surroundings: the neighboring texts, the project name, the date. Otherwise the paragraph you found still has to be put back into context by hand.

Searching by word and returning to the same date in the past are different ways of recalling an entry. For a personal archive both may be more use than a complicated system of tags. Putting a question to a whole collection of documents is the next, harder step: the answer will need specific fragments to check it against. Reviews about word search do not prove that a generalization like that will be accurate.

quotes.text: I've been using Todoist for at least seven years now and I have it well integrated into my daily life. It is the one place I can throw anything at any time and not have to think about it again. Wake up at 3am with a thought, add it and I know it's taken care of.

Ulysses ranks at the top end of professional writing programs. Among it's outstanding features are the all-in-one Library. Everything you've ever written (if you like), plus everything you are currently working on or ever will work on, is accessible from one window.

I've been using this app since I had an iphone 4! I love it, I can search certain words and it will show me every entry that contained that word. It even does throwbacks, shows you what you wrote on the same day a year ago.

placements.title: Searching by memory, not by file name

observations.title: Keeping an archive that outlives the phone
passages: Over time notes stop being just files: work decisions, a personal history and unfinished texts stay in them. That is why the ability to open an old archive has to be judged separately from how comfortable it is to make a new entry. Recent changes matter most, since they may not have reached the available copy yet.

The date of the last copy decides how much of the work can be brought back. If the backup runs once a month, a restored archive of many years can still lose the most recent important entries. The state of the copy should say how fresh it is and what is in it, not only that the feature is switched on.

Portability of the archive is a reason in its own right to pick a notepad for the long run. The person needs to open the texts and attachments without the old app, keeping the dates and the connections that matter to them. Checking one old item that has a photo in it will show more than the name of the format in the settings.

quotes.text: I don't write reviews usually but—in my opinion, this app deserves some public commendation. TEN YEARS I've been using this app now; I just checked. (Strangely, to the month! So call this my 'decade anniversary' review.) I always just used it simply and relied on it.

I did the latest update and all my notes got deleted from the last SEVEN years. If you have backups on in the app you can restore from there. BUT they only backup the first of every month. So I had lost one month of (important) entries.

TLDR; If you have been looking for a notebook app that is not a subscription with portable data and deeply integrated in the apple ecosystem system, this is it. I looked a long time at different note apps. I would not have found this if I hadn't been so particular.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Keeping an archive that outlives the phone”.

placements.title: Keeping an archive that outlives the phone

observations.title: Knowing where the latest edit is
passages: Local storage, a cloud copy and sync solve different problems. The first decides where the entry is, the second helps you recover, the third lets you continue the work on another device. A note being present on the phone says nothing yet about whether the latest edit reached the computer.

When a subscription ends, the person has to understand what will happen to what they have already written. In one review, entries that had built up over about a year and a half disappeared. The terms for reading and exporting your own archive have to be explained in advance; they are not the same as the terms for sync or for access to new features.

Moving local entries into a cloud changes the owner’s original choice. A move like that calls for a clear explanation and a way to take the material out. And being local and being encrypted are different properties: where something is stored says nothing in itself about who can read the data and how access is restored.

quotes.text: OneNote is phenomenal on my phone and Windows desktop. I use it all the time. The problem is I also have a Mac laptop. OneNote used to work on the Mac, but now is unusable on the Mac because it does not reliably save changes. This means I can't trust it anymore.

UPDATE. I really loved this app. I purchased a one-year membership after enjoying it for about six months. I did not renew as money was tight. Everything I had written since the beginning disappeared. I am so sad. About 18 months worth of entries.

The original app was never great but it worked and I could keep my content locally without using their cloud services. This new 3.0 major update forces you to upload all of your old notes to the cloud. After updating the app, they give you no choice.

placements.title: Knowing where the latest edit is

sections.title: Carrying the work on beyond the note
sections.intro: The material you have found is rarely the end goal. A meeting has to turn into agreement on the next steps, lecture notes into a review of the topic, sketches into a long text. This is where the scenarios appear that bring a person back into the app.

observations.title: Coming back to the right remark after a meeting
passages: A recording of a conversation is not wanted for the sake of one more file. The person wants to come back to a difficult term, a name or an agreement they had no time to write down. A transcript helps find that moment if it stays tied to the original audio and allows corrections.

A short start matters during the conversation itself: the app should not require a separate working environment to be set up at the moment of the meeting. Recording on the move and transcribing afterwards lets you separate taking part from preparing the outcome. At the same time, the fact that recording is happening has to be clear to the people in the room.

For someone who tries to take everything down word for word, the attention freed up may be the main benefit. But an automatic outcome has to be checked separately: was a decision actually made, who took the task on, and was a deadline named. The recording, the transcript and the edited summary have to stay distinguishable, so that the system’s guess does not turn into an agreement between the participants.

quotes.text: I've tried many meeting recorder and note-taking tool out there, and nothing comes close. The transcription quality is genuinely impressive - not the hedging "pretty good for AI" kind, but the kind where you scroll back through a dense technical discussion and find it got everything right.

I use Granola every single day and it has become indispensable to my workflow. On mobile, it's perfect for capturing conversations during walks and transcribing meetings on the go. The one-tap capture makes it effortless to start recording without breaking focus.

As the title already states, I have ADHD and Autism. I have a difficult time with note taking because I oftentimes want to write EVERYTHING down rather than key points. As you can imagine, this makes it difficult to stay focused on the actual topic.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Coming back to the right remark after a meeting”.

placements.title: Coming back to the right remark after a meeting

observations.title: Turning a chosen fragment into a question
passages: Lecture notes keep the explanation, while a card poses a short question for review. When the two live in different places, the wording has to be carried across and corrections have to be tracked separately. A link between them lets you return to the detailed material at the moment when the short answer is no longer enough.

Not every paragraph is worth turning into a question. Let the learner pick what is important, formulate the answer and open the original context. For a large collection of documents the reverse path is useful too: from a topic to the explanation you need. Then review carries the work with the notes forward instead of creating a second archive.

A large collection of PDFs and transcripts is not yet a ready deck for review. First the material has to be chosen, along with the question it answers. Once the original definition is corrected, the linked card should ask to be revisited: the convenience of automatic generation is not worth memorizing an out-of-date answer.

quotes.text: I started school again last month, and I was on the hunt for a program that would consolidate my notes all in one place. I am an organizational nut, and I needed a better system. Being an avid fan of Anki already, I somehow stumbled upon this program.

I used to have so many random notes in my notes app, or pages, or some random new app I'd try and delete within a few days and couldn't keep it all straight. I started using this for my foreign language studies because of its flash card feature.

If you've ever stared at a mountain of PDFs, research papers, meeting notes, or YouTube transcripts and thought, "There has to be a smarter way to make sense of all this," Google NotebookLM is your answer.

placements.title: Turning a chosen fragment into a question

observations.title: Passing the text to where the work will continue
passages: Sometimes the mobile notepad is the place of capture and the main work happens in another editor. In that scenario an internal system of folders can turn out to be an unnecessary intermediate stage. The person wants to write the thought down and continue it in the project they have already chosen, keeping the format they are used to.

Configurable actions are useful when their result is predictable: where the text will land, whether a file will be created or an existing one added to. Handing the text over should not erase the original before there is a confirmation you can read. Test a full fragment with headings and links: a short line will not reveal the loss of structure in transit.

A route can be very simple: add a work thought to one document, leave a personal one in the inbox, send a photo to the project folder. For a set like that you don’t have to ask anyone to write a script. Setting it up through actions people understand lowers the barrier to entry, and looking at the result after the first hand-off helps confirm that the headings, links and attachments arrived where they should.

quotes.text: I'm blown away by the power of the app. It's transforming my workflow. I'm constantly wishing that I could do this or that only to discover that it's already baked in or easy to add with a bit of simple scripting. I can't believe how customizable it is.

I love this app. Navigation is great, it supports [[backlinking]], ![embeds](), and #tags like a champ. I use Obsidian with iCloud and this pulls in all of my files with ease. My favorite feature is the customizable markdown extended keyboard.

placements.title: Passing the text to where the work will continue

conclusion.title: Choosing what people come back to an entry for
conclusion.body:
For a first product I would choose lecture notes linked to questions for review. There is a concrete continuation of the entry here, and direct examples of people finding it convenient to keep both parts together. On the material of a single topic you can test whether it is easier to prepare the questions, to return to the explanation and to update the card after the notes have been corrected.

But fast entry and the ability to take your own entries with you have to survive first. An automatic summary, a knowledge graph and a library of every format are not required for that test. Meetings and manuscripts are separate directions with different results. A new notes app should cut out one repeated piece of work, not simply offer one more place for people to move an old archive into.
